passage.title: Engines of the Open Ocean
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Passage
passage.text:
Every late summer, weather satellites track spinning cloud bands across the Atlantic Ocean. Most tropical storms weaken before they ever reach the southeastern coast. Yet a storm that crosses the Gulf Stream can gain speed in one night. The Gulf Stream is a fast ribbon of warm sea water flowing north from the tropics. To a big storm, this warm current acts like fuel in a giant heat engine.

Warm water feeds a storm through rapid evaporation. As strong winds sweep across the sea, warm mist rises into the core of the storm. When that mist climbs high into the cold sky, it turns to rain and lets off huge amounts of heat. That released heat warms the surrounding air and makes it rise even faster, dropping the air pressure near the waves. More outside air then rushes in to fill the gap. This fast flow spins the wall of clouds around the calm eye at ferocious speeds.

Even a fierce storm cannot keep its top wind speed for long. After churning for days, a mature storm often builds a second, wider ring of rain clouds outside its first eye. The inner eyewall, cut off from warm ocean moisture by this outer ring of storms, is gradually starved of energy by the expanding outer band. As the inner ring weakens and falls apart, the peak wind speeds drop for a full day.

This natural shift is called an eyewall replacement cycle. Peak winds near the center slow down during the swap. Still, the storm's wide wind field grows much broader. The outer ring slowly contracts inward to take the place of the old eye. If the hurricane is still floating over deep, warm Gulf Stream water when the new eyewall tightens, its winds can surge back to dangerous levels. If it moves over cooler shelf water instead, the storm stays weaker.

A few hours can decide if a storm hits land during a weak phase or a strong phase. For this reason, brave flight crews fly right through these tall cloud rings. They drop small tubes that check water heat and wind speed from the sky down to the sea. By tracking both the ocean heat below and the shifting eyewalls above, forecasters give coastal families clearer warnings before the wind arrives.

tier2Words.definition: the process in which liquid water turns into rising water vapor
tier2Words.contextClue: As strong winds sweep across the warm sea, warm mist rises into the core of the storm.
Falling air pressure pulls more air inward, spinning the cloud wall at dangerously fast speeds.

tier2Words.definition: fully developed or grown after a period of time
tier2Words.rootHint: Latin root maturus ('ripe or fully grown')

tier2Words.definition: draws inward or shrinks into a tighter space

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 3:

"The inner eyewall, cut off from warm ocean moisture by this outer ring of storms, is gradually starved of energy by the expanding outer band."

Based on the structure of the sentence, which part of the storm loses energy, and what causes that loss?

options.text: The expanding outer band loses energy because the inner eyewall blocks the warm ocean moisture.
options.childFeedback: This reverses the two cloud rings! The inner eyewall is the one that loses energy because the outer band cuts off its warm ocean moisture.

options.text: The inner eyewall loses energy because the expanding outer band cuts off its warm ocean moisture.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 3, the phrases 'cut off from warm ocean moisture by this outer ring' and 'starved of energy by the expanding outer band' show that the inner eyewall loses energy because the outer band blocks its moisture.

options.text: Warm ocean moisture loses energy because weather satellites block the outer ring of storms.
options.childFeedback: Weather satellites high in space only track the cloud bands in Paragraph 1—they never block a storm's ocean moisture.

options.text: Coastal forecasters starve the Gulf Stream of energy by dropping small sensor tubes into the waves.
options.childFeedback: The small tubes dropped by flight crews in Paragraph 5 only measure water heat and wind speed; they do not starve the Gulf Stream of energy.

questions.provingSentenceText: The inner eyewall, cut off from warm ocean moisture by this outer ring of storms, is gradually starved of energy by the expanding outer band.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 3, the phrases 'cut off from warm ocean moisture by this outer ring' and 'starved of energy by the expanding outer band' show that the inner eyewall loses energy because the outer band blocks its moisture.
questions.parentExplanation: In this passive construction, 'The inner eyewall' is the receiver of the passive verb 'is gradually starved of energy,' while 'by the expanding outer band' names the actor causing the energy loss.
questions.retryHint: Look at the subject ('The inner eyewall') and the 'by' phrases in Paragraph 3 to see what gets starved of energy and why.

questions.prompt:
Read these sentences from Paragraph 4:

"Still, the storm's wide wind field grows much broader. The outer ring slowly contracts inward to take the place of the old eye."

What does the word contracts mean as it is used in Paragraph 4?

options.text: Signs a written agreement with weather forecasters
options.childFeedback: A 'contract' can be a written paper agreement in other settings, but a ring of storm clouds cannot sign a paper agreement!

options.text: Splits apart into dozens of tiny rain showers
options.childFeedback: The inner ring is the one that weakens and falls apart in Paragraph 3, while the outer ring pulls inward to become the new eyewall.

options.text: Spreads outward until it covers the whole ocean
options.childFeedback: Spreading outward across the ocean is the opposite of 'contracts inward' and 'tightens' in Paragraph 4.

options.text: Tightens and pulls closer toward the center
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 4, 'contracts' means tightens and pulls closer toward the center, as shown by the clue 'contracts inward to take the place of the old eye' and 'when the new eyewall tightens.'

questions.provingSentenceText: The outer ring slowly contracts inward to take the place of the old eye.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 4, 'contracts' means tightens and pulls closer toward the center, as shown by the clue 'contracts inward to take the place of the old eye' and 'when the new eyewall tightens.'
questions.parentExplanation: The context clues 'inward to take the place of the old eye' and the subsequent phrase 'when the new eyewall tightens' show that 'contracts' means tightens or draws inward.
questions.retryHint: Look at the words 'contracts inward to take the place of the old eye' and 'when the new eyewall tightens' in Paragraph 4.

questions.prompt: Based on Paragraph 2, how does rising mist that turns to rain high in the sky increase wind speed near the waves?

options.text: It releases heat that makes air rise faster and lowers surface pressure, pulling more air inward.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 2 explains that when rising mist turns to rain high in the sky, it releases heat that makes air rise faster and lowers surface pressure, pulling more outside air rushing in.

options.text: It pushes warm Gulf Stream water back south toward the tropics.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 1 says the Gulf Stream flows north from the tropics, and rain inside a storm does not push the ocean current backward.

options.text: It freezes the ocean waves into solid ice so the wind can slide across them without friction.
options.childFeedback: Hurricanes feed on warm ocean water—the ocean waves never freeze into solid ice beneath a tropical storm.

options.text: It stops all evaporation from happening anywhere inside the storm's calm eye.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 2 begins by explaining that warm water feeds a storm through rapid evaporation, not by stopping evaporation.

questions.provingSentenceText: That released heat warms the surrounding air and makes it rise even faster, dropping the air pressure near the waves.
questions.childTip: Paragraph 2 explains that when rising mist turns to rain high in the sky, it releases heat that makes air rise faster and lowers surface pressure, pulling more outside air rushing in.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 2 explains the cause-and-effect chain: rising mist turns to rain and releases heat, which makes air rise faster and drops air pressure near the waves, drawing more outside air inward.
questions.retryHint: Read the third, fourth, and fifth sentences of Paragraph 2 to trace the chain reaction after the rising mist turns to rain.

questions.prompt: How does the author structure the end of Paragraph 4 to explain what happens after a new eyewall replaces the old one?

options.text: By listing every hurricane that has struck the southeastern coast over the past century
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 4 never lists historical hurricane names or dates; it explains the science of an eyewall replacement cycle.

options.text: By describing how pilots build airplanes strong enough to fly through heavy rain
options.childFeedback: Flight crews are mentioned in Paragraph 5, and neither paragraph explains how engineers build airplanes.

options.text: By contrasting what happens to the new eyewall over warm Gulf Stream water versus cooler shelf water
options.childFeedback: The last two sentences of Paragraph 4 use an 'If... If...' contrast to compare what happens when the new eyewall tightens over deep, warm Gulf Stream water (winds surge) versus cooler shelf water (the storm stays weaker).

options.text: By arguing that satellites are no longer useful for tracking summer storms
options.childFeedback: The author never claims satellites are useless; satellites track the cloud bands from above while flight crews check wind and heat inside the storm.

questions.provingSentenceText: If the hurricane is still floating over deep, warm Gulf Stream water when the new eyewall tightens, its winds can surge back to dangerous levels.
questions.childTip: The last two sentences of Paragraph 4 use an 'If... If...' contrast to compare what happens when the new eyewall tightens over deep, warm Gulf Stream water (winds surge) versus cooler shelf water (the storm stays weaker).
questions.parentExplanation: The end of Paragraph 4 uses parallel conditional ('If...') sentences to contrast two outcomes: re-strengthening over warm Gulf Stream water versus staying weaker over cooler shelf water.
questions.retryHint: Look at the two 'If' sentences at the end of Paragraph 4 to see the two different ocean conditions being compared.

questions.prompt: Part A: Based on the passage, why must meteorologists study both the ocean surface and the cloud rings during an eyewall replacement cycle?

options.text: Because flight crews cannot fly above the clouds when the sun is shining.
options.childFeedback: Flight crews fly right through tall storm cloud rings in Paragraph 5; sunshine never stops their weather planes.

options.text: Because sensor tubes can only measure wind speed if they land on a dry sandy beach.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 5 says crews drop small tubes 'from the sky down to the sea' to check water heat and wind speed, not onto a dry beach.

options.text: Because an outer eyewall always causes the Gulf Stream to reverse direction and flow south.
options.childFeedback: An outer eyewall only blocks moisture from reaching the inner eyewall—it never reverses the flow of the Gulf Stream.

options.text: Because the interaction between shifting eyewalls above and water heat below determines how strong the storm will be.
options.childFeedback: Paragraphs 4 and 5 explain that whether a storm hits land during a weak phase or surges back to a dangerous phase depends on both the shifting eyewalls above and the ocean water heat below.

questions.provingSentenceText: By tracking both the ocean heat below and the shifting eyewalls above, forecasters give coastal families clearer warnings before the wind arrives.
questions.childTip: Paragraphs 4 and 5 explain that whether a storm hits land during a weak phase or surges back to a dangerous phase depends on both the shifting eyewalls above and the ocean water heat below.
questions.parentExplanation: Across Paragraphs 3-5 (ELAGSE5RI3), the author explains that a hurricane's strength depends on both the stage of its eyewall replacement cycle and the warmth of the water beneath it.
questions.retryHint: Read Paragraph 5 to see why flight crews drop tubes from the cloud rings down to the sea and what two things forecasters track.

questions.prompt: Which quotation from the passage best supports the correct answer to Question 5?

options.text: "Every late summer, weather satellites track spinning cloud bands across the Atlantic Ocean."
options.childFeedback: This opening sentence from Paragraph 1 only mentions weather satellites tracking cloud bands, without connecting eyewalls and ocean heat.

options.text: "By tracking both the ocean heat below and the shifting eyewalls above, forecasters give coastal families clearer warnings before the wind arrives."
options.childFeedback: This final sentence from Paragraph 5 directly supports Question 5 by stating that tracking both the ocean heat below and the shifting eyewalls above lets forecasters give clearer warnings.

options.text: "Most tropical storms weaken before they ever reach the southeastern coast."
options.childFeedback: This general fact from Paragraph 1 does not explain why meteorologists must study both ocean heat and shifting eyewalls.

options.text: "After churning for days, a mature storm often builds a second, wider ring of rain clouds outside its first eye."
options.childFeedback: This sentence from Paragraph 3 only describes the outer ring of rain clouds, without mentioning the ocean heat below.

questions.provingSentenceText: By tracking both the ocean heat below and the shifting eyewalls above, forecasters give coastal families clearer warnings before the wind arrives.
questions.childTip: This final sentence from Paragraph 5 directly supports Question 5 by stating that tracking both the ocean heat below and the shifting eyewalls above lets forecasters give clearer warnings.
questions.parentExplanation: Option C directly quotes Paragraph 5, confirming that combining measurements of ocean heat and eyewall shifts enables accurate coastal warnings.
